item.title: Dogo Onsen Spring Festival — Guide
item.description: The Dogo Onsen Spring Festival (Dogo Onsen Matsuri) is the annual celebration of the historic hot-spring town of Dogo, held over several days in spring. Centred on the famous Dogo Onsen Honkan bathhouse and the surrounding arcade and streets, it fills the onsen quarter with traditional dances, music, costumed processions and events honouring the town’s long history and the gods of the hot spring. The atmospheric setting — the grand old wooden bathhouse, the shopping arcade and the hot-spring town in the fresh green of spring — makes it a charming, less overwhelming festival than the great summer events, and a lovely time to combine a soak at Dogo Onsen with a taste of local celebration in Matsuyama.

item.title: Kumamoto Hi no Kuni Matsuri — Guide
item.description: The Hi no Kuni Matsuri (‘Fire Country Festival’) is Kumamoto city’s biggest and liveliest summer celebration, held over several days in August. Its name reflects Kumamoto’s identity as the ‘Land of Fire’, tied to the great Aso volcano. The festival’s centrepiece is the huge ‘Otemoyan Sōodori’ — a mass street dance in which thousands of participants in colourful costumes, organised into teams, dance energetically through the downtown streets to the catchy strains of ‘Otemoyan’, a famous and much-loved Kumamoto folk song.

item.title: Matsuyama Summer Festival — Guide
item.description: The Matsuyama Summer Festival (Matsuyama Matsuri) is the city’s largest annual celebration, held over three evenings in mid-August. Its highlight is the ‘Yasakoi’ dance — teams of costumed dancers parade through the central streets performing an energetic, rhythmic routine, with a distinctive local flavour that has absorbed influences from samba and other styles into a joyful summer spectacle. Alongside the dancing, the festival brings food stalls, music and a buzzing street atmosphere to central Matsuyama, and is often rounded off with a fireworks display over the city.

item.title: Miyako Odori: Gion's Geiko and Maiko Spring Dances — Guide
item.description: The Miyako Odori, the ‘Dances of the Old Capital’, is the great annual public performance of the geiko and maiko of Gion Kobu, held throughout April since 1872. For a few weeks each spring, the geisha who normally perform only in private teahouses take to a theatre stage in a lavish, tightly choreographed production, with rows of maiko in matching seasonal kimono dancing to live traditional music, backed by painted scenery that changes with the seasons of the year.

item.title: Ohara Festival — Guide
item.description: The Ohara Festival (Ohara Matsuri) is Kagoshima city’s largest and liveliest festival, held every year in early November. Its centrepiece is a huge mass street dance in which around 20,000 participants — organised into teams from companies, schools and community groups, dressed in matching happi coats, yukata and colourful costumes — dance together down the city’s main streets to the infectious rhythm of local folk songs, above all the famous ‘Ohara-bushi’.

item.title: Takamatsu Summer Festival — Guide
item.description: The Takamatsu Festival (Takamatsu Matsuri) is the prefectural capital’s largest summer celebration, held over several days in mid-August. It fills the central streets and the harbour area with a lively mix of dance parades, music, performances, food and game stalls and a festive summer atmosphere, drawing crowds from across the region. Its grand finale is a spectacular fireworks display launched over Takamatsu’s harbour and the Seto Inland Sea, the bursts reflected in the calm water — one of the highlights of the Kagawa summer.

item.title: Yamaga Lantern Festival — Guide
item.description: The Yamaga Lantern Festival (Yamaga Tōrō Matsuri), held every year on 15–16 August, is one of the most enchanting summer festivals in Japan. Its unforgettable highlight is the ‘Sennin Tōrō Odori’ — the Thousand-Person Lantern Dance — in which around a thousand women in matching summer yukata dance slowly and gracefully through the night, each balancing a delicate golden paper lantern (kintōrō), lit from within, on her head. As they move in unison to haunting music, the sea of soft golden lights weaving through the darkness creates a scene of extraordinary, dreamlike beauty.

item.title: Koenji Awa Odori Guide: Tokyo's Biggest Summer Dance Festival
item.description: For two evenings every August, the laid-back western Tokyo neighbourhood of Koenji erupts into the city’s largest and most exhilarating dance festival. Some 10,000 dancers in traditional costume pour through the streets to the hypnotic, driving rhythm of shamisen, taiko drums, and flutes, while up to a million spectators line the route. This is the Koenji Awa Odori — the biggest awa odori celebration outside its birthplace in Tokushima, and one of the great experiences of a Tokyo summer.

item.title: Yosakoi Soran Festival Guide: Dates, Where to Watch & Access
item.description: Every June, Sapporo explodes with colour, music and motion for the Yosakoi Soran Festival — one of Japan’s most exhilarating dance events. Hundreds of teams, tens of thousands of dancers in bold costumes, surge through the streets and across stages, naruko clappers in hand, to powerful remixes of Hokkaido’s traditional “Soran Bushi” fishing song. Born only in 1992, the festival fuses Kochi’s yosakoi dance with Hokkaido’s sea-shanty heritage into a thrilling, modern spectacle that fills Odori Park and the city for several days.
